title: Building a Stronger Argument
text:
Academic writing depends on precise collocations that signal how strongly a claim is made. Writers often make a claim, but they must support it with evidence. A claim that is well supported is far more persuasive than one that is simply asserted.

Some phrases hedge a statement, such as 'it may suggest' or 'the data tend to show'. Such hedges are not signs of weakness; they show that the writer is aware of the limits of the evidence. Readers usually trust a writer who acknowledges those limits.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what must a writer do after making a claim?
What examples of hedging phrases does paragraph two give?
Why are hedges not signs of weakness, according to the passage?
options: They show awareness of the limits of the evidence
They replace the need for data

questions.text: What can be inferred about readers' trust in a writer?
options: Readers trust writers who claim absolute certainty
Readers tend to trust writers who acknowledge limits

vocabulary.definition: words that regularly occur together in a language
able to convince someone to accept an argument
a word or phrase that softens a statement

paragraph_translations: La escritura académica depende de colocaciones precisas que indican con qué fuerza se formula una afirmación. Los autores suelen hacer una afirmación, pero deben respaldarla con evidencia. Una afirmación bien respaldada es mucho más persuasiva que una simplemente afirmada.

Algunas frases atenúan una afirmación, como 'it may suggest' o 'the data tend to show'. Estos atenuantes no son señales de debilidad; muestran que el autor es consciente de los límites de la evidencia. Los lectores suelen confiar en un autor que reconoce esos límites.
